newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Winds, current reduce Venezuela oil spill's impact.
newsitem.headline: Winds, current reduce Venezuela oil spill's impact.

text.p: Favourable winds and currents appeared on Tuesday to have limited the environmental damage caused by a large oil spill off Venezuela's northwestern coast, officials said.
But some conservationists warned the bulk of the spill had yet to reach land.
About 11 miles (17.5 km) of sandy coastline on the western flank of the Gulf of Venezuela had been affected, but only 1 1/2 miles (2.5 km) was badly fouled.

Along a coastline extending some 12 miles (20 km) from the village of San Carlos to the small beach resort of Caimare Chico, white sand beaches were coated with black puddles and the stench of oil was strong. But there was no major slick.

"Perhaps its early days but it's very encouraging so far," said Tosh Moller, a senior technical advisor for London-based International Tanker Owners Pollution Federation, sent to assess damage claims from the spill.

The Greek-flagged Nissos Amorgos, carrying 476,000 barrels of heavy Venezuelan crude bound for Italy, ran aground on Friday in a shipping channel at the mouth of Lake Maracaibo, spilling about 25,000 barrels, industry officials said.
The spill grew to 60,000 barrels when the ship was moved east for repairs, the Venezuelan Navy said.
Hundreds of men used spades to scoop oil-stained sand off the polluted coastline on Tuesday.

"We have about 300 people cleaning the whole coast ... it's a time-consuming process, we have to be patient," said Ciro Gonzalez, local manager of environmental protection for Lagoven, a subsidiary of state oil giant Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA).
Environment Minister Rafael Martinez told Congress damage was less than initially feared and said the cleanup operation could be over for the peak Easter holiday period.
But conservationists monitoring the spill warned that its worst effects had not yet been seen.
Lenin Herrera, president of the Lake Maracaibo Conservation Institute (ICLAM), an autonomous body funded by the Environment Ministry, said only a tiny proportion of the oil had come ashore.
"Up to now what we are seeing (on the coast) is nothing like the total volume of crude oil," he told Reuters.
ICLAM biologist Nerva Morales said the pollution was worsening. "Today is twice as bad as yesterday and tomorrow will be worse," Morales said as she collected samples of clams from the beach.
Strong winds and an outgoing tide at the time of the accident had helped push the oil away from the entrance of Lake Maracaibo out to open sea, Herrera said.
